title: Git Internals: The Objects Under Your Commits
summary: A 10-page handwritten-notes carousel dissecting how Git actually stores history — blobs, trees, commits, tags, SHA-1 content addressing, refs, HEAD, reflog, and packfiles.

chapters.title: 1. The Big Idea: Content-Addressed Storage
points: Git is a key-value store: everything is an object looked up by the SHA-1 hash of its content
Object location: .git/objects/ab/cdef... — first 2 hex chars are the directory, rest is the filename
SHA-1 of an object = sha1("<type> <size>\0" + content) — the header includes type and byte length
Same content always produces the same SHA → identical files stored once, forever (deduplication for free)
Content addressing makes history tamper-evident: change a byte, the hash changes, every dependent object changes
Four object types: blob, tree, commit, tag — all stored in the same object database
Try it: echo 'hi' | git hash-object -w --stdin → prints the SHA and writes a loose object
git cat-file -p <sha> pretty-prints any object; git cat-file -t <sha> prints its type
Collision risk: SHA-1 is ~160 bits; practically safe, and Git now detects collision attacks (sha1dc)
Mental model: Git isn't diffs or deltas — it's snapshots named by hashes
git cat-file --batch-check < <sha list> to inspect many objects quickly

chapters.title: 2. Blobs: Storing File Content
points: Blob = raw file bytes + header, nothing else: no filename, no permissions, no timestamps
Filename and mode live in the tree, not the blob — rename a file and the blob is reused
git hash-object -w file.txt writes a blob without staging or committing anything
Deduplication: 100 files with identical content = 1 blob; git cat-file -s <sha> shows byte size
File mode is a tiny enum in trees: 100644 (file), 100755 (executable), 120000 (symlink), 160000 (gitlink/submodule)
Blob identity is content-only → Git tracks content, not files; 'a file' is just a path pointing at a blob in a tree
Editing one line creates a brand-new blob; the old blob still exists until garbage collection
git cat-file -p <blob-sha> dumps the raw content back out
Gotcha: git hash-object without -w only computes the hash, writes nothing
Binary files are blobs too — Git treats them as opaque bytes (diffs need special config)
Empty file = valid blob with SHA e69de29... (hash of empty content) — you'll see it constantly

chapters.title: 3. Trees: Snapshots of Directories
points: A tree = one directory snapshot: list of (mode, type, SHA, filename) entries
git cat-file -p <tree-sha> reads a tree; use git ls-tree <commit-ish> for human-friendly output
Trees point to blobs (files) and other trees (subdirectories) — the whole repo is a tree of trees
The root tree is what a commit points to; it recursively captures the entire working snapshot
Filenames are part of the tree entry, so a rename changes the tree but reuses the blob
Any unchanged file/subdirectory keeps its SHA → commits reuse huge subtrees, keeping repos small
Tree SHAs are content-addressed too: same directory contents anywhere in history = same tree
git write-tree builds a tree object from the current index — the index literally is the next tree
Inspect recursively: git ls-tree -r -t HEAD lists every tree and blob under it
Saw a 040000 mode? That's a directory entry (subtree), different from file modes
Gotcha: you rarely create trees by hand — git add updates the index, commit writes the tree

chapters.title: 4. Commits: Pointers With a Story
points: A commit object = tree SHA + parent commit SHA(s) + author/committer + timestamp + message
git cat-file -p HEAD shows the raw commit — do this once and internals click
First commit has no parent; a merge commit has 2+ parents — that's all a merge is structurally
The tree SHA pins the full snapshot at that moment; parents give you history as a linked list/DAG
Author vs committer: who wrote the change vs who applied it (rebases, patches via git am)
Timestamps are part of the hash input — same message + parents at a different time = different commit
Commits are immutable: amending or rebasing creates NEW commit objects; old ones linger until GC
git commit-tree <tree> -p <parent> -m 'msg' forges a commit by hand — great learning exercise
A 'branch' is NOT stored in the commit — it's just a ref pointing at a commit (next chapter)
Commit graph traversal: git log --graph --oneline --all visualizes the DAG
Gotcha: copying a commit SHA elsewhere fails if parent history isn't there — commits are only meaningful in context

chapters.title: 5. Annotated Tags vs Everything Else
points: Tag object = a commit SHA + tagger + date + message (+ GPG signature) — the 4th object type
git cat-file -p v1.0 on an annotated tag shows tagger, message, and the commit it points to
Lightweight tag = just a ref file containing a commit SHA — no object, no message, no signature
Annotated tags point at the tag object; the tag object points at the commit — one extra hop
Use annotated for releases: git tag -a v1.0 -m 'Release 1.0'; verify with git show v1.0
git tag -s adds a GPG signature inside the tag object — the release's cryptographic receipt
git tag -v v1.0 verifies the signature; signed tags are the backbone of verified releases
Gotcha: git push doesn't send tags by default — use git push --tags or push a specific tag
Gotcha: lightweight tags follow a moved commit silently; annotated tags freeze the moment
git describe uses tags to name commits like v1.2-3-gabc1234 (3 commits after v1.2)
Note: lightweight tags aren't 'wrong' — fine for temp bookmarks, wrong for releases

chapters.title: 6. Refs and HEAD: The Movable Pointers
points: A ref is a 41-byte file containing one SHA: .git/refs/heads/main literally IS the branch
Branch = movable pointer to a commit; creating one is writing one tiny file — branches are cheap
HEAD is a symbolic ref: file containing 'ref: refs/heads/main' — it points at a ref, which points at a commit
Detached HEAD: HEAD holds a raw SHA instead of a ref name — committing here orphans your work
git branch <name> = write a ref file; git checkout <name> = repoint HEAD; that's it
Namespaced refs: refs/heads/* (branches), refs/tags/*, refs/remotes/* (remote-tracking), refs/stash
Special refs outside namespaces: HEAD, ORIG_HEAD, FETCH_HEAD, MERGE_HEAD
git rev-parse HEAD resolves any ref to its raw SHA; git symbolic-ref HEAD shows what HEAD names
git update-ref refs/heads/main <sha> is the safe scripted way to move a branch (with locking)
Gotcha: deleting a branch deletes only the pointer — commits remain until reflog expiry and gc
Remote refs move only on fetch/push, which is why your origin/main can be 'behind' after others push

chapters.title: 7. The Reflog: Your Safety Net
points: Reflog = local journal of where each ref has pointed: one line per HEAD/ref movement
git reflog shows HEAD history; git reflog show <branch> shows that branch's history
Every entry is reachable: git checkout HEAD@{3} or git reset --hard HEAD@{2} jump back
Reflog syntax HEAD@{n} = n moves ago; HEAD@{2.hours.ago} = where HEAD was at that time
Rescuing 'lost' commits: git reflog → find the SHA before the mistake → git branch rescue <sha>
Why resets feel safe: git reset --hard only moves refs; reflog remembers the old position ~90 days
gc.reflogExpire (90d) and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (30d): after expiry, dropped commits become GC fodder
Gotcha: reflog is local-only — never pushed; it can't rescue commits from someone else's reset
Gotcha: a freshly cloned repo has a nearly empty reflog — no local history to rewind
git log -g walks commits in reflog order rather than topological order
Common save: git reset --hard HEAD@{1} to undo a bad reset you just ran

chapters.title: 8. Packfiles: Compression at Scale
points: Loose objects (one file per object) waste space and inodes → Git packs them into .git/objects/pack/*.pack
Packing triggers: git gc, git repack, push/fetch over smart HTTP & SSH, many loose objects
Pack index (.idx) maps SHA → byte offset in the .pack for O(1)-ish object lookup
Delta compression: similar blobs stored as delta against a base object — often just version N vs N+1 of a file
Deltas work across types: a blob may be stored against an unrelated-but-similar blob
git verify-pack -v reports pack contents, sizes, and chain depths — find your repo hogs
git gc packs and prunes; git count-objects -vH compares loose vs packed footprint
Lookup order: packfiles first (via idx), then loose objects — transparent to every command
Gotcha: objects pushed to a server arrive as a pack immediately; local edits stay loose until gc
Trade-off: deltas make storage tiny but reads require delta resolution — a deliberate CPU-for-space trade
Shallow clones (--depth) and partial clones (--filter=blob:none) skip pack data you don't need

chapters.title: 9. Common Mistakes & Recovery Playbook
points: Myth: 'git reset --hard deletes my work' — it only moves refs; reflog still holds the old SHA
Myth: 'force-push loses history forever' — on the receiving machine it does; on yours reflog has it
Detached-HEAD disaster: committed while detached, checked out elsewhere → grab SHA from reflog, branch it
git reset --hard <sha> vs git checkout <sha>: reset moves the branch, checkout moves only HEAD
Deleted a branch: git reflog show <branch> before it expires, or use fsck --lost-found
git fsck --unreachable finds dangling commits/blobs the reflog no longer protects — last-resort recovery
Amended/rebased commit 'vanished': it's still in reflog under ORIG_HEAD or the pre-move entry
Accidental git add of secrets: unstage ≠ removed; the blob is in the object DB — rewrite history (filter-repo) and rotate keys
Stash is ref-based too: dropped stash recoverable via git fsck --unreachable | grep commit
Habituating --force on push hides others' work — prefer --force-with-lease
Rule of thumb: anything committed is recoverable for ~30–90 days; anything only staged, less so (blobs still exist until gc)

chapters.title: 10. Summary: The Whole Model on One Page
points: The stack: blob (file bytes) → tree (directory snapshot) → commit (snapshot + parents) → tag (signed label)
Everything is content-addressed by SHA-1: same content = same object, everywhere, forever
Branches and tags are just files containing SHAs; HEAD is a pointer to a pointer — that's the entire 'branch' feature
git add writes blobs + updates index; git commit writes a tree + a commit and moves the ref
Reflog is your local undo journal; packfiles + deltas are the storage engine underneath
One command tour: hash-object → cat-file → write-tree → commit-tree → update-ref = Git's core in five primitives
Complexity cheat sheet: object lookup ~O(1) via pack idx; branch create O(1); log traverses the commit DAG
Immutability is the feature: hashes make history verifiable; movability of refs makes history editable
Reading list: Pro Git ch. 10 (Git Internals), git help gitobjectlayout, git help repository-layout
Exam yourself: what does .git/refs/heads/main contain? What's the difference between a tree and a commit?
Final habit: when lost — git reflog, git fsck, git cat-file. The object database almost never loses what you committed
